title: An omitted common cause in ice-cream and sunscreen sales
scenario_markdown: Across summer days, a beach retailer observes a positive regression slope between ice-cream sales and sunscreen sales. Temperature was not recorded. Hotter days plausibly increase demand for both products. The retailer did not randomly change ice-cream sales or assign treatments.
assumptions: The data are observational and temperature is a plausible common cause.
A plausible omitted variable is a hypothesis to investigate, not proof of the entire causal mechanism.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which explanation most directly challenges a causal interpretation of the slope?

options.text_markdown: Temperature may influence both sales series, creating association without an ice-cream-to-sunscreen causal effect.
A positive slope proves buying ice cream makes customers buy sunscreen.
options.hint_markdown: The observational relationship can arise through a common cause.

options.text_markdown: A significant p-value eliminates all omitted-variable explanations.
options.hint_markdown: Statistical significance is conditional on a model and does not establish causal identification.

stages.explanation_markdown: Temperature is a plausible confounder: it relates to the predictor and may independently affect the response. The slope can capture this omitted common influence.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which next step would help assess this concern?

options.text_markdown: Collect temperature and other justified variables, examine the adjusted association, and state the limits of observational control.
Change sales units from dollars to cents to remove confounding.
options.hint_markdown: Rescaling changes coefficients' units, not the causal structure.

options.text_markdown: Add random unrelated predictors until R-squared is large.
options.hint_markdown: Variables need a defensible causal or predictive role.

stages.explanation_markdown: Including temperature can test sensitivity to a plausible common cause, but measurement error and unmeasured factors can remain. Adjustment alone is not automatic proof of causation.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which business statement is defensible from the original regression?

options.text_markdown: Ice-cream and sunscreen sales are associated in these observations; the data alone do not establish that increasing ice-cream sales would raise sunscreen sales.
Doubling ice-cream sales will necessarily double sunscreen sales.
options.hint_markdown: The observational slope is not a guaranteed intervention effect or a fixed proportional law.

options.text_markdown: The association is impossible unless the relationship is causal.
options.hint_markdown: Common causes can generate association between two outcomes.

stages.explanation_markdown: A regression can support prediction under suitable validation while leaving causal attribution unresolved. A causal claim requires a design and assumptions that address confounding and the proposed intervention.
